name: Horuru
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only an ISO 639-3 change request; no descriptive material.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is phonemic. [p. 469] ... Fatamanue has two stress patterns as seen in some languages of Maluku. The majority of words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. Some stress falls on the final. But, the stress remains in its original position, even when plural or other suffixes are added. This stress pattern is similar to the Big Nambas's of Vanuatu (Fox 1979). Compare the two Fatamanue pairs below: ai 'tree': aí 'foot' (cf. u-ai 'my tree': aí-u 'my foot') / ana 'to shoot an arrow': aná 'child' (cf. si ána 'they shoot an arrow': si aná 'their child') / ata 'four': atá 'stir up' ... mata 'to die': matá 'an eye' ... utu 'louse': utú 'happiness' [p. 471]
new_statements.citation: Sakiyama, Osamu. 1999. Nominals of Fatamanue, Seram Maluku: A Subgrouping Argument in Central Malayo-Polynesian. Bulletin of the National Museum of Ethnology 24(3): 467-484.

But, the stress remains in its original position, even when plural or other suffixes are added. This stress pattern is similar to the Big Nambas's of Vanuatu (Fox 1979). Compare the two Fatamanu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic). Default/majority pattern is penultimate; a minority of lexical items carry final stress (marked with acute in the source). The lexically specified stress position is fixed to the root and does not move when plural or possessive suffixes are added (e.g. aí-u 'my foot' keeps final stress on the root; u-ai 'my tree' keeps penultimate). So: predominantly penultimate with a lexical class of final-stressed words; not derivable from syllable weight.
new_statements.exceptions: The final-stressed words are themselves the exception class; the source lists ten minimal pairs and notes (p. 474) that in the plural lists stems with final stress are marked only in the singular. No other exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on lexical roots; the suffixation examples (possessive and plural) show stress is root-anchored rather than computed on the suffixed word. Data from the Haruru dialect primarily (p. 468), with a few Yalahatan comparisons.
new_statements.identity_note: horu1241 'Horuru' is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 CR 2011-086 retired [hrr] and merged it into Yalahatan [jal] = Glottolog yala1266 'Yalahatan-Haruru-Awaiya' (Three Rivers, Nunusaku, Central Maluku, CMP Austronesian). 'Horuru' is the village name Haruru (locally [fululu]), the parent village of the language Sakiyama calls Fatamanue (also Atamanu), spoken at Haruru (~500) and Yalahatan (~700). The quoted statement is from Sakiyama 1999, which is primarily a description of the Haruru dialect, i.e. exactly the variety 'Horuru' named. The statement should be filed under yala1266 (also an uncatalogued target in, whose scan marked Sakiyama 1999 'not online'; it is in fact open access at the Minpaku repository), with horu1241 as a duplicate/retired code pointing to it, not as a separate catalog entry.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Establishes identity: Horuru's only reference was Voegelin 1965; the name is Haruru, one of the two villages (Yalahatan and Haruru) of the Yalahatan language, Three Rivers group, central Seram; cites Sakiyama 1999 as the description.

sources.note: Comparative-historical; treats Atamanu (Haruru, Yalahatan, Awaiya) as a subgroup member with wordlist reflexes (pp. 34-60). Its only stress statements (pp. 82-83) concern Asilulu vs Hoamoal languages (penultimate stress), not Atamanu. Silent on Atamanu/Horuru stress.
